title: Mark 11:1–11
context: Jesus approaches Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives and arranges, with prophetic foreknowledge, to ride a young donkey never ridden before. The crowds spread garments and branches and cry out words from Psalm 118, hailing the coming kingdom of David. Mark ends the scene quietly: Jesus looks around the temple and withdraws to Bethany. Arminian and Reformed readers agree this is a deliberate messianic act that echoes Zechariah 9:9, a humble king coming in peace.

verses.text: When they came near to Jerusalem, to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus sends two disciples from near Bethsphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives. Arminian readers note the deliberate staging: Jesus chooses the place and time of his entry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the Mount of Olives’ link with the Lord’s coming in Zechariah 14:4. Jesus moves toward Jerusalem knowingly, fulfilling his mission.

verses.text: and said to them, “Go your way into the village that is opposite you. Immediately as you enter into it, you will find a young donkey tied, on which no one has sat. Untie him and bring him.
verses.arminianNotes: He tells them they will find an unridden colt tied in the village. Arminian and Reformed readers agree this shows Jesus’ foreknowledge and recalls Zechariah 9:9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that an animal never ridden suits sacred use (compare Numbers 19:2). The king directs every detail.

verses.text: If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord needs him;’ and immediately he will send him back here.”
verses.arminianNotes: If asked, they are to say the Lord needs it and will send it back. Arminian readers see Jesus’ authority joined with courtesy: he borrows and returns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the title Lord. Whether it means Jesus himself or God, interpreters differ, but the claim of authority is clear.

verses.text: They went away, and found a young donkey tied at the door outside in the open street, and they untied him.
verses.arminianNotes: They find the colt tied by a door in the street and untie it. Arminian and Reformed readers agree the fulfillment matches Jesus’ word exactly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the reliability of Jesus’ word demonstrated in small things.

verses.text: Some of those who stood there asked them, “What are you doing, untying the young donkey?”
verses.arminianNotes: Bystanders ask why they are untying the colt. Arminian and Reformed readers agree Mark records the scene as Jesus predicted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s providence works through ordinary people and questions.

verses.text: They said to them just as Jesus had said, and they let them go.
verses.arminianNotes: They answer as Jesus said, and the people let them go. Arminian readers note the disciples’ simple obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that obedience to Christ’s word meets with the outcome he promised.

verses.text: They brought the young donkey to Jesus and threw their garments on it, and Jesus sat on it.
verses.arminianNotes: They lay garments on the colt and Jesus sits on it. Arminian and Reformed readers agree this is an act of royal homage (compare 2 Kings 9:13).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the humble king of Zechariah 9:9, coming not on a war horse but a donkey.

verses.text: Many spread their garments on the way, and others were cutting down branches from the trees and spreading them on the road.
verses.arminianNotes: Many spread garments and leafy branches on the road. Arminian and Reformed readers agree this is a festive, royal welcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the enthusiasm of the crowd, which Mark will soon contrast with the rejection of Jesus.

verses.text: Those who went in front and those who followed cried out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!
verses.arminianNotes: The crowds cry Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the Lord’s name, from Psalm 118. Arminian and Reformed readers agree the crowd hails Jesus as the coming one, though perhaps without understanding the cross ahead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hosanna, meaning save us, is a prayer that Jesus will answer in a way the crowd does not expect.

verses.text: Blessed is the kingdom of our father David that is coming in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!”
verses.arminianNotes: Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David. Arminian and Reformed readers agree the crowd expects a Davidic restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the kingdom truly arriving in Jesus, though through suffering rather than political triumph.

verses.text: Jesus entered into the temple in Jerusalem. When he had looked around at everything, it being now evening, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus enters the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves for Bethany at evening. Arminian readers note the quiet inspection that sets up the next day’s action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Lord coming to his temple (Malachi 3:1) and surveying it before judgment.
